segments.title: Why the R.1 became the Blackburn Blackburn
segments.summary: The R.1's doubled Blackburn name introduces two competing explanations before Major F. A. Bumpus is identified as its designer.
segments.body: One account, attributed to Jackson, links the name to the Lancashire town shared by the manufacturer. Admiralty documents preserve a plainer story: when the R.1 needed a name, it was given the maker's name twice. The first version is treated as charming but romantic, while the second explains the literal Blackburn Blackburn form. Major F. A. Bumpus is then identified as the designer, separating the aircraft's designation, manufacturer, name, and designer.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses the doubled Blackburn name and credits Major F. A. Bumpus.

segments.title: Dart components simplified Fleet Air Arm spares
segments.summary: The R.1 used a two-bay biplane layout and components shared with the Blackburn Dart to simplify Fleet Air Arm spares holdings.
segments.body: The aircraft used fabric-covered wood and metal construction, folding wings, and a 450-horsepower Napier Lion IIB twelve-cylinder water-cooled engine installed as a detachable power unit. Its Dart-type louvred engine bay had controllable shutters. Lengths of steel tube fitted into joint clusters machined from solid material formed the centre structure, with subassemblies bolted to that nucleus. The mainplanes, tail unit, and control surfaces apart from the rudder were interchangeable with the Blackburn Dart. This commonality simplified the Fleet Air Arm's spares holdings.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the R.1's construction, Napier Lion installation, and interchangeability with the Dart.

segments.title: Cabin space for long reconnaissance sorties
segments.summary: A deeper, semi-monocoque fuselage provided enclosed working space for the R.1's reconnaissance crew on long sorties.
segments.body: Behind its steel centre section, the R.1 had a wider semi-monocoque fuselage with cabin accommodation for two crew members during long reconnaissance sorties. The wireless operator-gunner worked forward, with his equipment mounted above a folding table. A rearward extension of the cabin roof shielded the navigator-observer from the slipstream as he moved into the open rear cockpit. From there he could use a sextant, rangefinder, or camera, while the forward position supported wireless communication and gunnery.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the enlarged cabin and the wireless operator-gunner and navigator-observer positions.

segments.title: Deck-landing visibility and defensive guns
segments.summary: The R.1's cockpit cut-out and sloping cowling improved the pilot's view of the carrier deck while its crew carried forward and rearward-firing guns.
segments.body: The pilot sat high in a cut-out at the leading edge of the top wing's centre section. Decking ahead of him was cut away to clear the control wheel, with the gap closed by a Triplex windscreen. The sharply sloping engine cowling improved his view of the carrier deck during landing. A port-side Vickers gun fired through the airscrew with 500 rounds, while a Lewis gun on a Scarff ring behind the rear cockpit covered rearward and downward arcs with three ammunition drums.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the pilot's deck view and lists the Vickers and Lewis gun positions.

segments.title: A full-depth fuselage for three crew and fuel
segments.summary: The R.1 remained a three-seater despite four crew positions, using a full-depth fuselage and up to 90 gallons of fuel for its reconnaissance role.
segments.body: The R.1 had four working positions but only three crew members, an arrangement described as little more comfortable than the three Avro Bison prototypes N153 to N155 ordered to the same specification. Its upper-wing centre section bolted directly to the cabin roof, so the deep fuselage filled the entire gap between the wings. This full-depth form grew from design studies for the broad-fuselage Swift IV and Blackburn civil ten-seater. Main fuel sat in a saddle tank over the centre of gravity and behind the pilot, while two streamlined upper-wing tanks raised total capacity to 90 gallons.

evidence.note: The transcript covers the three-seat arrangement, full-depth fuselage, and 90-gallon fuel system.

segments.title: Landing gear for early carrier arresting wires
segments.summary: Because it was not a torpedo carrier, the R.1 used conventional strengthened landing gear with claws for early deck arresting wires.
segments.body: Unlike the torpedo-carrying Dart, the R.1 did not need the Dart's undercarriage arrangement. It used conventional wheel-and-axle gear, strengthened centrally and braced with extra struts for deck landings at a high rate of descent. Claws engaged the fore-and-aft arresting wires used at the time. The landing gear therefore had to meet both the structural demands of carrier operations and the requirements of the contemporary arresting system.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the R.1's landing gear with the Dart's and describes its arresting-wire claws.
